content: In biological taxonomy, a type is a reference point that permanently links a name to a taxon. Depending on the nomenclature code applied, the type can be a specimen, culture, illustration, description, or taxon. The concept of a type is used differently in botany and zoology, leading to some complexity in its application. Botany In botanical nomenclature, a type (or typus) is the element to which the name of a taxon is permanently attached. A botanical name, by itself, is merely a phrase (usually one to three words) and requires a type to clarify what it applies to. The type fixes the name to a specific taxon. In botany, a type can either be a specimen or an illustration. A specimen is a real plant (or parts of a plant) that has been preserved and curated in a herbarium or a similar facility for fungi. In some cases, an illustration may serve as a type, particularly in historical contexts where transporting and preserving dried plants was challenging. For example: Detailed botanical drawings or paintings from the early days of plant taxonomy often served as types when physical specimens were lost or damaged. Illustrations of microscopic plants, which are difficult to preserve or locate on microscope slides, may also serve as types. It is important to note that a type only fixes a name to a single representative of a taxon. It does not determine the circumscription (the extent or boundaries) of the taxon. For instance, the common dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) is a controversial taxon. Some botanists consider it to consist of over a hundred species, while others regard it as a single species. Regardless of the circumscription, the type of the name Taraxacum officinale remains the same. The circumscription of a taxon is determined by a taxonomist in a publication. Typically, only species or infraspecific taxa have their own types. For new taxa published after January 1, 1958, the type cannot be an illustration. A genus almost always has the same type as one of its species, often referred to unofficially as the type species. Similarly, a family has the same type as one of its genera, often called the type genus. The International Code of Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN) provides a detailed listing of types, with the holotype being the most important. Zoology In zoological nomenclature, a type refers to a specimen or taxon that serves as the objective standard for determining the application of a name. The name-bearing type provides a reference point for the name of a nominal taxon. Definitions A type specimen is an individual or fossil that serves as a name-bearing type for a species. For example, the type specimen for Homo neanderthalensis is Neanderthal-1, discovered in 1856 in Germany, consisting of a skullcap, thigh bones, part of a pelvis, ribs, and arm bones. A type species is the nominal species that serves as the name-bearing type of a genus or subgenus. A type genus is the nominal genus that serves as the name-bearing type of a family-group taxon. The type series includes all specimens cited in a taxon's formal description unless explicitly excluded. Use of Types When describing a new taxon, biologists may examine multiple specimens, but under the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN), a single type must be designated. If a single specimen is designated as the type in the original description, it is called a holotype. The holotype is typically stored in a museum or collection for future examination. The type description should include a discussion of similarities and differences with related species and the location of the type specimen. The geographical origin of a type specimen is known as its type locality. Zoological collections, maintained by universities and museums, ensure that types are preserved and available for examination. While there is only one holotype, other formally defined types include: Paratype: Additional specimens listed in the type series but not name-bearing types. Neotype: A specimen later designated as the type when the original holotype is lost or destroyed, or when no original type was cited. Syntype: Any of two or more specimens listed in a species description when no holotype was designated. Lectotype: A specimen later selected to serve as the single type from a set of syntypes. Paralectotype: Any additional specimen from a set of syntypes after a lectotype has been designated. Hapantotype: A special case in protists where the type consists of multiple specimens representing distinct life cycle stages, treated collectively as a single entity. These various types are necessary because many species descriptions date back centuries, and holotype designation was not always practiced. Original type specimens may have been lost, poorly preserved, or destroyed. The validity of a species name may depend on the availability of original type specimens or the clarity of the description. The ICZN, established in 1961, did not always require a type specimen, and many type-less species exist, such as Homo sapiens. Recent species descriptions sometimes involve releasing the type specimen back into the wild, as in the case of the Bullo Burti Bush-shrike (Laniarius liberatus), where DNA sequences were used instead of a preserved specimen. If future questions arise, a neotype may need to be designated. Type Species Each genus must have a designated type species. The description of a genus is usually based on its type species, modified by the features of other included species. The generic name is permanently associated with the name-bearing type of its type species. Ideally, the type species exemplifies the essential characteristics of the genus, but this is not a requirement of the Code. If the type species is later found to belong to a pre-existing genus, all constituent species must either be moved to the pre-existing genus or dissociated from the original type species and given a new generic name. Type Genus A type genus is the genus from which the name of a family or subfamily is derived. It is not necessarily the most representative genus but is often the earliest described, largest, or best-known genus. Family names are based on type genera, even if the type genus has become a synonym.
